data.title: Route Overview
paragraphs: The route begins with acclimatisation in Cusco before dropping into the Sacred Valley, where lower elevations, farm terraces, markets, and village communities create a more gradual relationship with the Andes. Community visits are built around real activities rather than costume performance.

Camila gives textiles a central role because weaving, natural dyes, agriculture, and identity intersect throughout the valley. Archaeological sites remain important, but they are sequenced alongside living communities so the past never overwhelms the present.
highlights: Two-night acclimatisation window in Cusco before a busier valley programme.
Community-led textile and agricultural experiences in the Sacred Valley.
Maras and Moray explored with landscape and farming context.
Ollantaytambo and Machu Picchu approached without turning the route into a sprint.

data.title: Suggested Packing & Preparation
items: Warm layers for cold mornings and strong Andean sun later in the day.
Comfortable walking shoes for stone streets and uneven archaeological paths.
Sun protection and reusable water bottle for high-altitude dryness.
Respectful clothing for community-hosted visits and ceremonies.

data.quote: The valley is not an archaeological corridor. It is a living place where weaving, farming, language, and memory continue beside the ruins.

data.title: ALTITUDE & COMMUNITY NOTE
data.text: Altitude tolerance differs greatly between travellers. Community experiences should also be booked through local hosts who control the format, timing, photography expectations, and whether a visit is appropriate at all.

data.title: The Living Valley Beyond the Ruins
paragraphs: Machu Picchu matters, but it gains depth after days spent with terraces, salt ponds, weaving groups, markets, and valley towns. The journey gives the present enough space to stand beside the past.
That balance is what makes the Sacred Valley feel inhabited rather than preserved behind glass.

items.question: Can Sacred Valley Weaves & Andean Trails be tailored to our dates and interests?
paragraphs: Yes. Camila Huamán’s route is a design framework rather than a fixed group departure. Stays, activity intensity, and specialist visits can be adjusted while protecting the geographic logic of the journey.
items.listTitle: Common ways to personalise the route:
listItems: Add or remove a night at the most important base.
Reduce walking or replace it with a lower-intensity alternative.
Add a specialist food, craft, wildlife, or photography focus where locally appropriate.

items.question: What is the best season for this journey?
paragraphs: Altitude tolerance differs greatly between travellers. Community experiences should also be booked through local hosts who control the format, timing, photography expectations, and whether a visit is appropriate at all.

items.question: What is included in the estimated journey budget?
listItems: Handpicked accommodation described in the final confirmed proposal.
Private or pre-arranged ground transfers listed in the route.
Specialist guiding and scheduled cultural or nature experiences.
On-ground coordination for the confirmed itinerary.

items.question: How physically demanding is the itinerary?
paragraphs: The default pace is described as acclimatised. Walking, altitude, wildlife activity, or outdoor intensity varies by region, so the final version should be adjusted to the traveller’s fitness, health, and comfort.
listItems: Alternative or shorter activity options are used where practical.
Weather and local conditions can change the day plan.

items.question: How far in advance should we plan?
paragraphs: For small lodges, specialist guides, rail or ferry seats, light-aircraft sectors, or permit-sensitive experiences, planning several months ahead gives the best flexibility. The exact lead time depends on season and destination.

items.question: How are reservations confirmed and scheduled?
paragraphs: Once the final route, accommodation, and specialist experiences are approved, a 30% confirmation deposit is used to secure services. The remaining balance is normally due 45 days before arrival unless a supplier requires different terms.

items.question: What is the policy for date changes or cancellations?
paragraphs: We try to shift dates or restructure the route whenever suppliers allow, but remote lodges, permits, flights, ferries, and specialist appointments may carry their own non-refundable conditions.
listItems: 60+ days before arrival: refund or credit is calculated after non-refundable supplier costs.
30–59 days before arrival: partial refund or rescheduling credit depends on confirmed supplier terms.
Less than 30 days before arrival: cancellation follows the individual confirmed service conditions.
